scope: Second current-guidance resolution pass across selected conflicting records with complete retained stems/options.
policy: Do not invent a missing option or clinical detail.
Assign verifiedAnswer only when the retained stem/options support a current single-best answer.
When current guidance shows the item is multi-answer, under-specified, or missing the best action, keep verifiedAnswer null and non-publishable.

items.reason: Prerenal volume depletion can produce both FENa <1% and concentrated urine/high specific gravity. The source already states both A and B are compatible. The retained single-best-answer structure is therefore invalid without rewriting.
references: Standard pediatric prerenal AKI physiology and urinary-index interpretation

items.reason: Once HUS with oligoanuria is present, fluid therapy must be individualized. Respiratory distress can represent fluid overload, in which case additional fluid may be harmful; volume expansion is appropriate only for true hypovolemia. The retained stem does not establish intravascular volume status, so A cannot be verified as a universal next step.
references: Management of hemolytic-uremic syndrome in children: careful restriction after oligoanuria/fluid overload

items.reason: For asymptomatic stage 1 hypertension, the AAP pathway calls for repeat auscultatory BP in 1-2 weeks; if still stage 1 at the second visit, check upper/lower-extremity BP and repeat in 3 months. ABPM is used after persistent stage 1 hypertension over 3 visits. Because the retained stem describes the second high reading two weeks later and the next recommended step is not among the choices, option A should not be forced.
references: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline for Screening and Management of High Blood Pressure in Children and Adolescents

items.reason: Current rickets guidance recommends an initial biochemical panel including calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH, creatinine and 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Several retained choices are therefore essential components, while 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is not a routine first-line screening test. The question cannot support one unique answer as written.

A shocked neonate requires rapid stabilization with ongoing reassessment and, when sepsis is suspected, prompt empiric antimicrobials. Fluids are titrated to hemodynamic status and stopped if overload develops; bicarbonate and prostaglandin are context-specific rather than routine. None of the retained choices cleanly represents this approach, and 'IV fluid only' is not adequate.

Current pediatric septic-shock guidance emphasizes heart rate, blood pressure, capillary refill, extremity temperature, pulse quality, mental status and urine output, with POCUS/advanced monitoring when available. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is not used as a standard 'late sign' discriminator. The retained options do not contain the clinically important late sign of hypotension and should not be modern-graded.

Fibrinogen and fibrin-degradation products can both be abnormal in DIC and in advanced liver disease and are not reliable single discriminators. The source itself notes a missing factor-VIII framing, and modern interpretation requires the entire clinical/laboratory pattern. No retained option can be promoted safely.

For a lower-risk BRUE, AAP guidance supports discharge after appropriate observation with family education and CPR resources and recommends against initiating home cardiorespiratory monitoring. Home monitoring may be appropriate in selected higher-risk infants or persistent apnea conditions. Because the retained stem does not define BRUE risk or the underlying apnea disorder, no single discharge option can be verified for all cases; the recalled home pulse-oximetry answer should not be promoted.
references: AAP BRUE guideline and Pediatric Care Online BRUE guidance

summary.note: This batch primarily removes false certainty: current guidance shows these eight items cannot be safely graded as retained.
